rv.q: Michael Grandage's robustly elegant production guides us confidently through Raicek's appealingly murky mixture of sex, power and professional status.
Still, Raicek's interpretation is bracing enough to make you forget the production's flimsier aspects.
This contemporary renovation looks fabulous, but you long for the rich strangeness of the original.
There are moments of great intensity, mostly in the scenes featuring Fleetwood, and real candescence to the writing at its best.
Ultimately Raicek has created as many problems as she's solved in trying to 'fix' the original story.
Instead of busting free of the original, the chic, effortful result proves an intriguing but frustrating half-way house.
But none of it gels. Blazing recriminations are interspersed with clotted dialogue that's achingly right-on.
It is a puzzle that Michael Grandage, fleetest of directors, was drawn to this script, which makes actors shrivel.
It's an idea rich with potential, but the result feels curiously wooden and inauthentic, even with Ewan McGregor in the lead.

I'd love to be able to report that this reframing proves illuminating – but while it's a relief not to be presented with two female roles that, deriving from Ibsen's template, could so easily amount to embittered, dutiful spouse and manic pixie dream girl, Raicek's innovations still feel pretty boilerplate.
But really, it's a load of old nonsense.
You're left wondering how this play made it to the West End, and why Grandage and McGregor decided to take a gamble on it.
Now, a sharp exploration of women and empowerment, My Master Builder, in its comedy and drive, is an exhilarating show.
My Master Builder is not the most radical interpretation of Ibsen, but it is an homage to the original, while constructing its own identity.
Dramatically, this is pure gold. It's a long wait but it's worth it.

None of these people is seems really likeable. Henry seems a sad figure set against the rest of them. He may be pretentious—calling his chapel a “star shafted portal from life into the celestial afterlife,” his unconsummated relationship with young Mathilde “the bright star in the dark tunnel of my life”—but, despite the highfaluting language, h...
There's no denying the talent on the stage at Wyndham's, and the cast do a sound job of keeping this cumbersome thing moving along.

My Master Builder is seductive to the eye throughout, but for a play steeped in second chances and the notion of returning, metaphorically speaking, to the emotional well, this study in 'the tragic wreckage of the past' exerts insufficient hold over the present.
The real problem with the play is that it's all a bit dull and grandiose and Grandage's direction is a bit flabby – too much tell and not enough show.
The reworking doesn't work. As the evening progresses, it becomes so weird and distancing that it is hard to care about its outcome.
Kate Fleetwood is fantastic, steals the show; Elizabeth Debicki mournfully watchable, Ajala's Ragnar an amusing prat.
